Case Vignette: "Lena"

Lena is a 38-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who has been in a committed relationship with her partner, David, for the past five years. She is a high-performing stock broker at a mid-sized firm in the city. She presents as articulate and professional, but there is a palpable tension beneath her composed surface.

The trauma began about fourteen months ago. It started subtly. Lena was working late, as she often did, monitoring the Asian markets. A new client-a man in his early 40s-had been referred to her. He was charming, well-spoken, and initially seemed like a solid portfolio. After their first few meetings, he began sending her emails late at night, commenting on her trades. Then, he started sending flowers to her office with notes that felt less like gratitude and more like declarations. "I know you work late. I think about you while you work." Lena felt a chill, but she dismissed it as a socially awkward client.

She told David about it, and they laughed it off. But the behavior escalated. The man began appearing at the coffee shop she visited every morning. He would be standing across the street from her building when she left for lunch. He knew her schedule. He knew her route home. Lena's daily commute, once a time to decompress from the market's volatility, became a ritual of hypervigilance. She started taking a different route home every night, a three-hour detour through back roads. She stopped going to the coffee shop.

The turning point was when she found a single, white rose on the driver's side door handle of her car in the underground parking garage. There was no note, but she knew. That night, she couldn't sleep. She felt a crawling sensation on her skin, as if he were in the room. She made David install three deadbolts on their apartment door and a motion-sensor camera in the hallway. She started sleeping with a small, tactical flashlight David had bought for camping, holding it under her pillow.

Lena's work, once her sanctuary of control, has become a battlefield. She is still a top broker, but the cost is immense. She cannot concentrate in her open-plan office. She feels exposed. She has moved her desk three times, now sitting with her back to a wall. She has installed a privacy screen on her monitor, not for proprietary data, but because she feels like she is being watched. She has become irritable with colleagues, snapping at them when they approach her from behind. She has stopped trading the volatile, high-reward stocks she was known for, favoring safer, less demanding positions. She says she feels "dumbed down," but she cannot tolerate the adrenaline of a fast trade anymore-it feels too much like the fear.

The most intrusive symptom is a recurring, sensory flashback. In quiet moments, especially when she is driving alone or trying to fall asleep, she smells the faint, cloying scent of the white roses. It is so real that she gags. She has checked her car for flowers dozens of times. She avoids the floral section of the grocery store.

Her relationship with David is strained. He is supportive, but he doesn't understand why she can't just "let it go" now that the man has been arrested for violating a restraining order. Lena feels a deep, isolating guilt. She blames herself for being "too friendly" with the client, for not recognizing the signs sooner. She has stopped going to the gym, stopped seeing her friends. She feels safest only in the small, windowless bathroom of her apartment, where she can lock the door and sit on the floor, her back against the tub. She has been there for hours at a time.

She recently told me, "I used to love the chaos of the market. I was good at it. Now, the only chaos I can feel is inside my head. I'm not scared of losing money anymore. I'm scared of losing myself."
